newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Budapest bourse ends firmer in lower turnover.
newsitem.headline: Budapest bourse ends firmer in lower turnover.

text.p: Gainers outnumbered losers on the Budapest Stock Exchange on Friday leaving the bourse in positive tone but traders said turnover was subdued before the release of an important U.S. indicator.
The BUX index finished at 5,500.25 points, up 35.49.
BUX futures strengthened for all maturities, by between 30.50 and 97.50 points. June BUX closed at 5,850, up 97.50.
"If the U.S. data are good we'll go upward, if they're bad nothing good looks for us," said Balazs Szabo of Eastbrokers.
U.S. March PPI figures made a surprise jump and this, in addition with stronger first-quarter retail sales might increase the chance of another rate hike.
Traders said earlier the Dow's movement has perhaps been the most important driving factor on the Hungarian market recently, in the lack of major domestic news.
On Friday oil company MOL advanced to 3,080 forints before retreating to close at 3,060, up 30, in what traders said was triggered by local demand.
Plastics firm Pannonplast rose to a record high of 8,700 forints, up 200, after announcing its dividend plan.
The company plans to pay 90 forints dividend on a share, which have 100 forint face value, on the 1996 earnings, against 70 forints the year before.
Trading turnover was not particularly strong on Friday but analysts remain optimistic on the market's stability on grounds of recent developments.

"The first was the Postabank crisis which, although had some effects on the market, really did not hit the market very hard," said Spencer Jakab, Budapest-based analyst at CS First Boston. "It did not hit the currency (forint) at all."
In late February Postabank clients withdrew deposits worth over 20 billion forints triggered by rumours.
The second factor, Jakab said, was the steep fall of the Dow Jones index on two days around Easter, after which the Hungarian market lost 95 points. "That (95 points) is nothing."

"The main point in the fact is, I think, this market is probably the most stable among central European markets," Jakab said. "Conventional wisdom says that it should be the least stable because it has the highest percentage foreign involvement and it has the most GDRs."
That has not been the case, however, he said, adding the Hungarian market was probably the least volatile.
